sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: **FaithWall** puts a sleep verse on your iPhone lock screen: find the verse, pick it, and the app applies it as your wallpaper through an Apple Shortcut. Start with Psalm 4:8. All eleven verses below fit under the clock at full size, one verse at a time.

sections.text: The best **Bible verses for sleep** are short, name the night plainly, and read in one glance before the phone goes face down. Psalm 4:8 is the classic: lie down in peace, and sleep. FaithWall keeps the verse you pick on your lock screen until you choose another, so it is the last line you read at night. Below are eleven King James verses in two groups, for restful nights and sleepless ones, each checked for fit. For the wider system, see the [daily Scripture lock screen guide](/daily-scripture-lock-screen).
Short Bible verses for sleep, rest and safety

These six are for an ordinary night. Each names sleep, rest or keeping in its own words, so it makes sense alone on a screen. Word counts come from the site's own KJV text, and each one sets in three to five lines.

items: Psalm 4:8 (19 words): "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety."
Proverbs 3:24 (20 words): "When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet."
Psalm 3:5 (13 words): "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the Lord sustained me."
Psalm 121:4 (10 words): "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep."
Exodus 33:14 (15 words): "And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest."
Matthew 11:28 (17 words): "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

sections.text: **Psalm 4:8 is the one I would set first.** Its psalm opens in distress and still ends in sleep, because the safety rests on the Lord, not on a calm night. Psalm 3:5, headed as David's psalm from when he fled from Absalom, is its morning answer. For nights you work late, Psalm 127:2 runs 26 words and five lines and ends in "he giveth his beloved sleep."
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety.
If fear of the dark keeps you up, Psalm 91:5 answers the terror by night in 18 words, and the [Psalm 91 wallpaper guide](/blog/psalm-91-wallpaper-iphone) checks that psalm verse by verse.
How to set a sleep verse with FaithWall

Setting a verse takes a few taps, and it stays on the lock screen until you pick another. The app places the text below the clock and applies it through an Apple Shortcut, so there is nothing to crop before bed.

items: Download FaithWall.
Choose the wallpaper setup.
Search for your verse, or open Psalms, chapter 4, in the built-in Bible browser, and pick it in KJV or any of the 24 translations.
The app runs an Apple Shortcut that sets it as your wallpaper; iOS shows Shortcuts for a moment.
For a darker background or another text style, tap Update Wallpaper Now in Settings.

sections.content: **Rather start with a single image?** The free [wallpaper maker](/bible-verse-wallpaper-maker) on this site turns a pasted verse into one PNG at iPhone or Pro Max size. For night, its Pure black style is the darkest choice, white serif text on a flat black background, and Dark gradient is the softer one. Set the download from Photos. It holds that one verse until you make another.

sections.text: Still choosing an app? The [ranked list of lock screen Bible apps](/best-bible-verse-lock-screen-apps) sets them side by side.
Bible verses for sleepless nights

Some nights the trouble is a mind that won't stop, not the dark. These five were written by people awake in bed, and they say so. Use them when the screen lights up at 2am and you need a line that meets you there.

items: Psalm 63:6 (15 words): "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches."
Psalm 4:4 (18 words): "Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah."
Psalm 116:7 (15 words): "Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee."
Psalm 139:12 (24 words): "Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee."
Psalm 30:5 (24 words): "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."

sections.text: **Psalm 63:6 turns the night watches into prayer**, and at four lines it reads in one glance. Psalm 77:4 names sleeplessness most exactly: "Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak." Read it; don't set it. Alone on a screen it stops at the trouble; the psalm only turns to remembering at verses 10 and 11.
When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.

The phone is often part of the night. 41% of U.S. adults say their smartphone hurts the amount of sleep they get, per Pew Research Center's 2026 smartphone survey; 5% say it helps. A verse doesn't change that. It changes what you read in the second before you put the phone down.
If worry keeps you awake more than the night itself, the [lock screen verses for anxiety](/blog/lock-screen-verses-for-anxiety) gather ten short lines for fear.

sections.text: How long can a bedtime verse be?

Keep it to about 24 words, six lines at most; longer, and a verse stops reading in one glance. It comes from running each verse through the site's wallpaper maker code on November 26, 2026, at iPhone size (1179 × 2556 pixels) and Pro Max size (1290 × 2796), in Pure black and Dark gradient.

All eleven set at full type size. The maker keeps the top 35% of the screen clear for the clock, date and widgets, and the bottom 12% for the flashlight and camera buttons, then sizes the verse to the space between. In Pure black the counts run:

items: Three lines: Psalm 3:5, Psalm 121:4 and Exodus 33:14, plus Psalm 77:4.
Four lines: Psalm 4:8, Matthew 11:28, Psalm 63:6, Psalm 4:4 and Psalm 116:7, plus Psalm 91:5.
Five lines: Proverbs 3:24 and Psalm 139:12, plus Psalm 127:2.
Six lines: Psalm 30:5, the same 24 words as Psalm 139:12, which wrap into one line more.

sections.text: Dark gradient sets DM Sans, a wider sans-serif, and adds a line to Exodus 33:14 and Psalm 139:12. Pro Max changes no counts. A pair also fits, Psalm 4:8 with Proverbs 3:24 at 39 words in eight lines, but that is two glances. Psalm 42:8, the song in the night, is the one I left off: 29 words, seven lines.

sections.title: The last screen and the first
sections.content: The screen you see last at night is the one you see first when you pick the phone up again. A verse set there gets read at both ends of the night, with no app to open and no page to find in the dark.

sections.text: Where a bedtime verse image goes wrong

Most sleep-verse images online are made for a feed: a whole passage over a bright starry photo. On a lock screen the clock lands on the first line, the sky glares in a dark room, and the text shrinks. **Bible verses for sleep** only work there if you can read them half awake.

**FaithWall handles the part that goes wrong.** You choose the verse, the app places it below the clock in your style and applies it, and it stays until you choose another. Keep Psalm 4:8 for ordinary weeks and Psalm 63:6 for long nights. Of all the **Bible verses for sleep**, the right one is the one you can read with your eyes half closed.
